promo-cal-sliver.title: Sized to fit is 3 mm short #shorts
promo-cal-sliver.description:
File → Settings → Show print bleed. There is the dashed line, just outside the page edge. Now I drop a photo in and size it to the page. Looks right. Edge to edge, nothing hanging over, very tidy.

And that is the mistake — because the page edge is not where the paper gets cut. The cut happens somewhere between the page edge and that dashed line, and no two copies get cut in exactly the same place.

So on this copy you get a white line down the right. On the next one, along the bottom. Twelve months, thirteen pages, every one of them a gamble.

📄 Free print card: https://geniusjunkie.net/get-photo-calendar-print-card/

promo-cal-drag.title: The fix is one drag #shorts
promo-cal-drag.description:
Canva's own instruction when bleed is showing: "resize or stretch your background to cover them."

So pull the photo out past the dashed line on all four sides. Now the photo overshoots the cut everywhere, and wherever the blade lands there is photograph under it.

That is what bleed is for. Canva adds 0.125 inches — 3.175 millimetres — on all sides for products that trim or get cut, and you cannot change it: fixed, their print specifications.

It costs you three millimetres of picture and it saves the whole calendar.

promo-cal-pixels.title: 2,500 pixels before you crop #shorts
promo-cal-pixels.description:
You need the photo to be about two and a half thousand pixels on its long edge for an A4 page. That is the number to check. Not megapixels, not how it looks on your phone — the pixel dimensions, in your file browser.

A photo straight off a modern phone is comfortably over that. The ones that fail are the copies: anything that came through a messaging app, anything downloaded off social media, anything that was emailed.

Those are compressed on the way, often down to around sixteen hundred pixels, and you cannot tell by looking at them on a screen. Go back to the original — the version in your camera roll, not the one somebody sent you back.

promo-cal-kitchen.title: A calendar is read from across a kitchen #shorts
promo-cal-kitchen.description:
A calendar is not read at arm's length. It is read from across a kitchen.

So zoom out until the page is about the size of a playing card, and then stand back from the screen.

What should survive: the photograph, the shape of the grid, and — crucially — this month's number block still reading as a block of numbers rather than grey fuzz.

If the dates have dissolved, they are too small or too light. Make them bigger before you make them prettier. A thin, elegant numeral at eight point is useless on a kitchen wall.
